teaser: Paris, 1900: a room hung with the same bridge, over and over. Visitors wondered where the sky had gone.

lesson.text: Late in 1900, people walking into Paul Durand-Ruel's gallery in Paris found something odd on the walls. About a dozen canvases showed one and the same thing: a wooden footbridge over a lily pond. Same spot, same angle, almost the same size.

Many visitors were charmed. Others were puzzled, even a little uneasy. Where was the sky? Where could the eye escape? One bridge would have been a landscape. A dozen in a row looked like an experiment, and that is exactly what it was.

Monet had been working this way for a decade. He would choose one motif, a word painters use for their chosen subject, and paint it under changing light: haystacks first, then poplars, then the front of Rouen Cathedral. The subject stayed put. What he was really painting was the hour and the weather.

For the Rouen Cathedral series Monet had rented rooms facing the church and worked away from home for weeks. For the bridge he only had to cross the road at the bottom of his flower garden. He had built this motif himself.
The painting you are looking at is one of that dozen, made in the summer of 1899. Monet chose a tall canvas for it, about 93 by 74 centimeters (36 by 29 inches), and stacked the view in three layers.

lesson.title: Three layers
lesson.text: Travel down the canvas from top to bottom.

spots.title: A wall of leaves
spots.text: Willows and shrubs fill the top with flickering yellow-green, pink and rust. Not one stroke of blue: the foliage closes the view like a curtain.

spots.title: The bridge
spots.text: Pale lilac and green rails arch across the middle. Through them you see more greenery, so the bridge acts as a screen, not a road leading anywhere.

spots.title: The pond
spots.text: Strips of pink and white lily pads alternate with dark vertical reflections. The water takes up half the picture and climbs the canvas like a carpet.

lesson.text: Curtain, screen, carpet. Each layer is nearly flat, and they sit one above the other more than one behind the other. A viewer in 1900 expected a landscape to open like a window. This one stays close to the surface, closer to a woven tapestry.
In a series, the subject repeats so that the light can change. Seeing several versions together is part of the work.

Compare this canvas with its siblings and it stands out for its warmth. Others in the group are cool and green. Here, reds and pinks run through the reflections and the far bank, as if the afternoon were late and the sun low.

1899 had begun badly for Monet. His old friend, the painter Alfred Sisley, died in January, and his stepdaughter Suzanne died days later, in February. He spent that summer in the garden, painting the pond.

spots.title: Yellow lilies
spots.text: A cluster of butter-yellow blooms at the left edge, the brightest notes on the water.

spots.title: The central post
spots.text: Monet sets this upright just right of center. Its lilac paint is thick and dry, dragged so that the canvas texture shows.

spots.title: Upside-down trees
spots.text: Vertical streaks of dark green and red between the lily pads: the trees on the bank, reflected in the water.

spots.title: Under the arch
spots.text: A dark hollow of shade below the bridge, with a fan of reeds beside it. It is the deepest point of the picture.

spots.title: Red at the bottom
spots.text: Streaks of brick red run under the nearest pads. Monet repeats this red at the top of the canvas, tying the two ends together.

spots.title: Signed in red
spots.text: “Claude Monet 99”, written in the same warm red he used in the water around it.

lesson.text: Two American collectors were not puzzled at all. Louisine Havemeyer and her husband Henry, a sugar magnate, bought this canvas soon after the show, guided by their friend the painter Mary Cassatt. Louisine left it to the Metropolitan Museum in 1929.

Monet came back to this bridge near the end of his life, around 1920, when cataracts had clouded his eyes. In those late versions the bridge almost dissolves into tangled strokes of red, orange and brown.

So here is a question to carry with you. If the same bridge can be green and cool in one canvas, pink and warm in the next, and burning red twenty years on, which one shows what the bridge really looked like?

quiz.question: What surprised visitors to Durand-Ruel's gallery in 1900?
options: About a dozen canvases showed the same bridge
quiz.explanation: Monet exhibited the bridge views as a series.

quiz.question: What is a motif?
quiz.explanation: The lesson defines motif as the subject a painter chooses.

quiz.question: In a Monet series, what changes from canvas to canvas?
quiz.explanation: The subject stays the same so the changing light becomes the real theme.

quiz.question: How did this painting reach the Metropolitan Museum?
options: Monet gave it to the museum
Louisine Havemeyer left it to the museum in 1929
It was found in a Paris attic
quiz.explanation: The Havemeyers bought it and Louisine bequeathed it.

quiz.question: What sets this version apart from others in the group?
quiz.explanation: Reds and pinks run through the water and the bank.

facts.text: The top of the painting shows a strip of blue sky.
facts.explanation: Foliage fills the top of the canvas completely.

facts.text: Before the bridge, Monet had painted series of haystacks and of Rouen Cathedral.
facts.explanation: He had worked in series for about a decade.

facts.text: Monet had to travel far from home to paint this bridge.
facts.explanation: It stood in his own garden at Giverny.
